summary:
Our project helps mission planners compare landing sites at the Moon’s south pole. A crater rim can block a rover’s view of Earth, and nearby sites can receive sunlight at different times. Both factors shape when a solar-powered rover can operate and communicate.

The website explains these challenges and offers a downloadable simulator. Users can select locations on the Moon, explore the surrounding terrain, and compare timelines showing when each site receives sunlight and has a direct line of sight to Earth. This makes it easier to spot periods when a rover would need to rely on stored energy or postpone tasks that require live commands.

A planned relay module will use modeled orbits for Queqiao-2 and Okina to estimate which satellite could bridge each gap in direct contact and for how long. Together, these tools help users evaluate where to land, when to operate, and when a mission would benefit from a communications relay.
details:
CisLunar is a lunar mission-planning prototype built around a deceptively simple question: where on the Moon should we operate, and when?

On the Moon, moving a rover only a few kilometres, or shifting the start of an operation by a few hours or days, can significantly change the conditions a mission experiences. A crater floor may remain in shadow while a nearby ridge receives sunlight. A site with a clear view of Earth may maintain direct communications, while another location just beyond the local horizon may require a relay satellite.

CisLunar brings these effects together so users can compare their operational consequences directly.

What we built

Users can select known lunar sites, such as Apollo 15, or choose any point on the lunar surface using selenographic latitude and longitude. They can define an exact UTC start time, move through the simulation with a time slider, and inspect the surrounding terrain in a 3D view with contour lines and an elevation scale.

The core of CisLunar is an A/B comparison system. Users can compare two locations at the same time, or the same location at two different dates. Both scenarios use the same simulation duration and time step, allowing sunlight and communications conditions to be compared on a common timeline.

For each site, the simulator evaluates the geometry of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar horizon. This distinction matters: being on the Earth-facing hemisphere does not automatically guarantee communications. Lunar curvature, the observer’s position, nearby mountains and crater walls, and the changing apparent position of Earth can all determine whether Earth is actually above the local horizon.

The simulation summarizes operationally useful quantities such as total time in sunlight, the longest continuous shadow interval, periods of direct Earth visibility, and the times at which the Sun or Earth rises above or falls below the local horizon.

The communications timeline then separates three possible states: direct-to-Earth communication, relay-assisted communication, and no available route. A direct link requires Earth to be visible from the lunar site. A relay link requires simultaneous line of sight from the surface site to the satellite and from the satellite toward Earth.

This makes an important difference visible. Two sites that appear geographically close can have very different communications histories. One may retain continuous direct Earth visibility, while another may periodically lose Earth behind the terrain or lunar horizon and depend on a relay during those intervals.

How we designed it

The central idea behind CisLunar is to connect geometry to operational consequences.

Instead of showing terrain, illumination, and communications as separate datasets, the interface lets the user move from one to the next as part of the same decision. A user can identify a promising ridge in the 3D terrain model, compare it with a nearby crater floor, and then see exactly when their sunlight or communications conditions begin to diverge.

The illumination model considers the direction of the Sun relative to the site and its surrounding terrain. A location may therefore enter shadow before the Sun falls below an ideal spherical horizon if a nearby ridge blocks it.

Earth visibility is treated in a similar way. The relevant quantity is not simply whether a location is on the lunar near side, but the elevation of Earth above the site's local horizon. That elevation changes with time because the apparent position of Earth in the lunar sky changes through lunar libration and orbital geometry. Local terrain can further raise the effective horizon and block an otherwise geometrically visible Earth.

Relay communications introduce another layer of geometry. CisLunar can demonstrate relay concepts using modeled spacecraft trajectories, including spacecraft such as Queqiao-2 and historical lunar relay-orbit examples. For a relay route to exist, the satellite must be visible from the lunar surface while also maintaining a usable geometry toward Earth.

The current simulator focuses primarily on geometric availability. A real communications link would require additional considerations including antenna orientation and gain, operating frequencies, transmitter power, receiver sensitivity, link margin, spacecraft compatibility, Earth ground-station visibility and scheduling, and network availability. CisLunar therefore identifies possible communication paths rather than guaranteeing a complete radio link.

The accuracy of these predictions also depends on the quality of the underlying data. Terrain resolution determines how well small ridges and crater walls are represented, while the simulation time step limits how precisely horizon-crossing events can be timed.

For higher-fidelity versions of the system, lunar topography can be derived from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation data, while solar, terrestrial, lunar, and spacecraft geometry can be calculated using authoritative ephemerides such as JPL Horizons or NASA/JPL SPICE kernels.

Who it helps

CisLunar is designed both as an educational tool and as an early-stage mission-planning environment.

Students can use it to explore why the Moon's geography affects power and communications instead of treating the lunar surface as a smooth sphere.

Mission designers can use the same concepts to screen candidate operating sites before moving to higher-fidelity analysis. A team could compare nearby landing or rover locations, identify the longest shadow interval for further battery analysis, determine when direct Earth communication disappears, or locate communications gaps before scheduling an operation that requires real-time commanding.

The goal is not to replace detailed illumination, orbital, or telecommunications software. It is to make the underlying trade-offs visible early enough that users can understand why one site or one date may be operationally better than another.

Companion website

We also developed a bilingual HTML, CSS, and JavaScript companion website that explains the physics behind CisLunar.

Its interactive demonstrations show how the Moon itself and local terrain can block a direct signal to Earth, and how a relay satellite can provide an alternative path. Lunar case studies illustrate environments such as crater floors, elevated ridges, polar regions, limb locations, and far-side sites.

A guided tutorial then walks users through their first A/B comparison, connecting what they see on the lunar map and 3D terrain view with the illumination and communications timelines below.

Together, the simulator and companion website emphasize one central idea:

On the Moon, choosing a location is also choosing its horizon—and that horizon determines when a mission can see the Sun, see Earth, and communicate.
